planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in part to full shade; this French selection is grown for its more refined, deeply cut leaf lobes rather than any difference in hardiness from the species.

directions: Rue Ledan is a European selection of bear's breeches valued for its narrower, more finely divided leaf lobes, which give the clump a lacier, less coarse texture than typical seed-grown Acanthus mollis while retaining the same bold overall scale. It forms the familiar large rosette of glossy, deeply lobed foliage that spreads slowly from thick, fleshy roots, eventually naturalizing into substantial colonies under high shade from trees or walls. In early summer it sends up tall, dramatic flower spikes of hooded white-and-mauve blooms well above the foliage, attracting bees and adding vertical structure to a shaded border. Divide congested clumps in spring, and expect any root fragments left in the ground to resprout, since the species regenerates readily from its roots.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container specimens in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in part to full shade; direct sun scorches and fades the white leaf margins faster than on the green-leaved species.

directions: Tasmanian Angel is a variegated sport of bear's breeches, its broad, deeply lobed leaves irregularly brushed and margined in creamy white against a dark green ground, making it a striking focal point in a shaded bed long before the flower spikes appear. It is slower and generally more compact than the plain green species, since variegated growth is less vigorous, but it carries the same coarse, architectural leaf form prized in Mediterranean-style plantings. Tall spikes of hooded white-and-dusky-purple flowers rise above the foliage in early summer when the plant is well established. Because the pale leaf tissue is more prone to sunburn and winter desiccation than solid-green forms, give it steady moisture, shelter from hot afternoon sun, and a protective mulch over winter at the cooler end of its range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in partial to deep shade in well-drained soil; site away from natural areas, since seed-grown plants of this species can escape into hammocks and forest understory in the Gulf South.

directions: Alba is a fruit-color form of coral ardisia that replaces the species' usual bright coral-red berries with clusters of pale ivory-white fruit, held beneath the same dark, glossy, wavy-edged evergreen leaves, giving winter displays a cooler, understated look in a shaded border. Like the species it tolerates dry, root-filled shade beneath established trees where few flowering shrubs persist, and produces small white summer flowers ahead of the developing fruit. Because coral ardisia is classified as invasive in Florida and other Gulf Coast states, grow this form only where fruit can be removed before it ripens and drops, or in a contained bed away from natural woodlands. Otherwise, culture matches the green-fruited species: consistent moisture while establishing, then good drought tolerance once rooted in.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring after all danger of frost, in sun to deep shade in moist, well-drained soil; this tropical species is severely damaged below freezing and is a listed invasive species — avoid planting near natural areas in Florida and Hawaii, where it is restricted or prohibited.

directions: Shoebutton ardisia is a glossy-leaved tropical shrub to small tree, grown historically in South Florida as a tough salt- and shade-tolerant hedge before its invasive habit was recognized. Clusters of small, star-shaped pink flowers appear along the stems through the warm months, followed by round berries that ripen from green through red to a glossy dark purple-black, hanging in profusion against the thick, leathery, elliptic leaves. It tolerates deep shade as well as full sun, making it adaptable to the understory conditions where many ornamentals struggle, but this same toughness lets birds spread seed widely into wetlands and hammocks. Because it is listed as a Category I invasive species in Florida and a noxious invader in Hawaii, it should not be planted in those regions and is included here for identification and historical-landscape reference only, not as a planting recommendation.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants
